title: SIDBOX CoderGirl Quick Reference and Beginner Guides
source: SIDBOX SDK headers and firmware Core (13 Oct 2026); Stage 25 IPC SDK extensions; Stage 3.23 V1 Game Engine/Advanced Platformer guides (16 Oct 2026)

SBOS_CreateWindow.summary: Create a CoderGirl GUI window. Pass a pointer to a CGWindow handle, position, size, title, and SBX_WF_* flags. Register its event procedure with SBOS_SetWindowProc().
SBOS_CreateWindow.notes: Keep the returned window handle for gadget creation and later window operations. In generated Designer applications, the window and its callback are created for you.

SBOS_CloseWindow.summary: Close the window identified by its CGWindow handle.

SBOS_SetWindowProc.summary: Install the window event procedure for GUI gadget, window, keyboard and other CGMessage_t events.
SBOS_SetWindowProc.notes: For V2 firmware, the OS invokes the callback through the applet-private stack bridge.

SBOS_WindowToFront.summary: Raise an existing window in the GUI Z-order.

SBOS_WindowToBack.summary: Move an existing window behind other normal windows.

SBOS_WindowSetFocus.summary: Give input focus to a window.

SBOS_WindowSetApplicationTitle.summary: Replace the application title shown by the window.

SetApplicationTitle.summary: Replace the application title shown by the window.

SBOS_WindowDisable.summary: Disable input interaction for a window.

WindowMouseBusy.summary: Set or query the mouse-busy indicator for an individual window.

WindowMouseIsBusy.summary: Set or query the mouse-busy indicator for an individual window.

SetMouseBusy.summary: Switch the OS pointer into busy or normal appearance.

SetMouseNormal.summary: Switch the OS pointer into busy or normal appearance.

SBX_WIN_DEFAULT.summary: Standard window flag combination: visible, moveable, titled, close/minimise/maximise controls, resizable and screen-bounded.

SBX_WF_VISIBLE.summary: Make a newly created window visible.
SBX_WF_VISIBLE.notes: Combine SBX_WF_* flags using bitwise OR (|).

SBX_WF_CLOSE.summary: Show a close control in the window title bar.

SBX_WF_MOVEABLE.summary: Allow the user to drag a window.

SBX_WF_RESIZABLE.summary: Allow the window to be resized.

SBX_WF_SCREENBOUND.summary: Constrain window movement to the physical display boundaries.

SBX_WF_ZORDER.summary: Participate in normal window Z-order behaviour.

CGMessage_t.summary: Event structure sent to the window callback. Important fields: mtype, winhnd, gadget, eventClass and event parameters a/b/c/d.
CGMessage_t.notes: The message pointer is callback-scoped; do not retain it after the callback returns.

CGWindowProcRes.summary: Return code for a window event handler. Use CGPROC_HANDLED for events you handled, CGPROC_DEFAULT for normal processing.

CGPROC_DEFAULT.summary: Return this from a window procedure to permit normal/default event handling.

CGPROC_HANDLED.summary: Return this when your application has handled the event.

CGEVT_WIN_CLOSE_REQUEST.summary: User requested that a window be closed. Handle it in the window procedure; close and free timers or other owned resources as appropriate.

CGEVT_GAD_ACTIVATED.summary: A GUI gadget has been activated (for example, a button). Compare m->gadget with your saved gadget handle.

CGEVT_GAD_SLIDERVAL_CHANGED.summary: Slider value changed. Read the slider value with SBOS_SliderGetValue().

CGEVT_GAD_CHECKBOX_CHANGED.summary: Checkbox state changed. Read it with SBOS_CheckboxGetState().

CGEVT_MENU_SELECTED.summary: A menu item was selected; configure and use the menu callback mechanism for item-specific actions.

SBOS_CreateLabel.notes: A 1x1 rectangle for a full-width label is not sufficient when overlapping windows trigger dirty-region repainting.

SBOS_CreateCheckbox.summary: Create a checkbox with an initial checked state.

SBOS_CreateRadioButton.summary: Create a radio button with group number and initial checked state.

SBOS_CreateSlider.summary: Create a slider using orientation and minimum/maximum values.

SBOS_CreateScrollbar.summary: Create a scrollbar with orientation, value range and small/large step sizes.

SBOS_CreateTextBox.summary: Create a single-line text-editing gadget. tb_flags chooses textbox behaviour.

SBOS_CreateTextArea.summary: Create a multi-line text area for longer editable text.

SBOS_CreateListBox.summary: Create a scrollable ListBox. Fill an ItemLists_t model and attach it with SBOS_ListboxAttachItemlist().

API_IPC.summary: V2 IPC function table appended after uart1 in the root API. Functions: self(), find(path_or_unique_filename), send(), receive(), pending().
API_IPC.notes: Requires firmware and SDK with Stage 25 IPC. The GUI Designer virtual Messenger component provides code-free sending and cooperative automatic reception.

SIDBOX_IPC_MESSAGE.summary: OS-copied IPC payload: sender instance ID, application-defined type, data length and up to 64 payload bytes.
SIDBOX_IPC_MESSAGE.notes: Payload is raw bytes, NOT necessarily a NUL-terminated C string. Copy at most 64 bytes and add a terminator when displaying text.

SIDBOX_IPC_MAX_DATA.summary: Maximum IPC payload size, currently 64 bytes.

SIDBOX_IPC_QUEUE_DEPTH.summary: Maximum messages waiting in one receiving applet mailbox, currently 8.

SIDBOX_IPC_OK.summary: IPC return code indicating successful send or receive.

SIDBOX_IPC_EMPTY.summary: Receive found no pending message; normal for nonblocking polling.

SIDBOX_IPC_BAD_ARG.summary: Invalid IPC argument, including a payload larger than 64 bytes.

SIDBOX_IPC_NO_CONTEXT.summary: The caller has no valid applet execution context.

SIDBOX_IPC_NO_RECIPIENT.summary: No live receiving applet matches the requested target/instance ID.

SIDBOX_IPC_QUEUE_FULL.summary: Recipient already has eight pending messages; try later.

SIDBOX_IPC_NO_MEMORY.summary: Firmware could not allocate mailbox memory.

API_Root.summary: Root API table at the SIDBOX OS interface. V2 applets use the fixed SRAM API pointer; the SDK provides macro API.
API_Root.notes: Never change member ordering. New tables must be appended to preserve older applet ABI offsets.

guides.title: 01 - Welcome to SIDBOX and CoderGirl
guides.summary: CoderGirl is the computer program used to write software for SIDBOX. SIDBOX is the device that runs the finished programs. A small program running on SIDBOX is called an applet. A GUI applet has windows and controls such as buttons and labels.
guides.notes:
A quick vocabulary guide:
• IDE: the editor used to write, design and build programs.
• SDK: the headers and libraries that let programs use SIDBOX features.
• GUI: graphical user interface — windows, buttons and other controls.
• Gadget: the name used for a GUI control.
• Source code: C instructions written or generated for an applet.
• Build/compile: turn source code into a runnable .app file.
• .sbui: a GUI Designer layout file.
Start with a small V2 GUI applet; no previous SIDBOX programming is required.
guides.example:
/* Common files in a GUI applet project:
   myapp.proj       project settings
   mainwindow.sbui   editable window design
   mainwindow.c      C code generated by Designer
   myapp.app         finished program for SIDBOX
*/

guides.title: 02 - Make a first GUI applet
guides.summary: Create a simple window that says Hello SIDBOX. This exercise uses GUI Designer, so there is no need to write a window procedure from scratch.
guides.notes:
1. In CoderGirl, create a GUI project.
2. Select the relocatable ARM ELF (V2/CGARM) applet format in project settings.
3. Open GUI Designer for the project window.
4. Add a Label gadget to the window. Set its visible text to Hello SIDBOX.
5. Save the .sbui design and generate its C source using Designer.
6. Build the project to create a .app file.
7. Copy that .app to the SIDBOX SD card and launch it.
If the build reports an error, read the first compiler error rather than the last one. Subsequent errors may be consequences of the first.
guides.example:
/* No C needs to be typed for this first exercise.
   GUI Designer creates the window and label code.
   The label's Text property is: Hello SIDBOX
*/

guides.title: 03 - Understand the Designer and generated code
guides.summary: The canvas shows where gadgets will appear. Select a gadget to edit its properties. The Designer saves the layout as .sbui and generates C source when requested.
guides.notes:
A gadget has a C variable name (such as lbl1 or btn1). Code uses that name to refer to the gadget. Designer also generates named callbacks — functions that run when an event happens.
IMPORTANT: Add handwritten code only inside a generated USER block, because code outside those blocks can be replaced when the design is regenerated. Save the .sbui before regenerating source.

guides.title: 04 - Add a label and change its text
guides.summary: A Label shows text on a window. Its C variable lets a button, timer or message callback change that text later.
guides.notes:
1. In Designer, add a Label and give it a name such as lbl1.
2. Set its Text property to Ready.
3. Make the label wide enough for the words you want to display.
4. Generate the C source.
5. To update it from code, use the example inside an appropriate callback USER block.
Why size matters: a 1×1-pixel label can look correct initially but have text disappear during partial screen repainting. Use realistic width and height.
guides.example:
/* Inside a generated callback USER block: */
SBOS_LabelSetText(lbl1, "Hello from SIDBOX!");

guides.title: 05 - Make a button do something
guides.summary: A button runs its Activate callback when clicked. The easiest first button changes a label on the same window.
guides.notes:
1. Add a Label named lbl1 and a Button named btn1 in Designer.
2. Give the Button visible text such as Click Me.
3. Save and generate the C source.
4. Find the generated On_btn1_Activate callback.
5. Put the example in that callback’s USER block.
6. Build and run. Clicking the button should change the label.
The Designer manages the button-event connection; beginners do not need to write a complete window-message dispatcher.
guides.example:
/* Inside On_btn1_Activate(...) USER block: */
SBOS_LabelSetText(lbl1, "You clicked it!");

guides.title: 06 - Learn a little C without being overwhelmed
guides.summary: CoderGirl applets are written in C. A variable stores a value, a function performs work, and an if statement chooses what to do.
guides.notes:
The example declares an integer named count. The = sign assigns a value. count++ adds one. The if statement tests a condition. Text between quotation marks is a string. A semicolon ends most statements.
A callback is an ordinary C function that CoderGirl calls for an event. Small snippets are most useful when placed in a generated USER block; they are not whole applets.
guides.example:
int count = 0;              /* create a number */
count++;                   /* increase by one */
if (count == 1) {          /* compare with 1 */
    dbug("First press");   /* write debug output */
}

guides.title: 07 - Build, launch and fix the first error
guides.summary: Building creates a .app file for SIDBOX. A compiler error means CoderGirl could not finish the build; it does not mean the SIDBOX hardware is broken.
guides.notes:
1. Save the .sbui and generate the C code.
2. Build the project in the IDE using its configured V2 CGARM backend.
3. If the build succeeds, locate the generated .app named in the build output.
4. Copy the .app to the SIDBOX SD card and start it on the device.
5. If the build fails, open the reported filename and line number and fix the FIRST error, then build again.
Common causes: a misspelled gadget variable, a missing semicolon, code pasted outside a function, or an SDK newer/older than the firmware.
guides.example:
/* Two typical compiler errors:

   error: expected ';' before '}'
   -> A statement may be missing a semicolon.

   error: 'lbl1' undeclared
   -> Check the gadget's actual C variable name.

   Compiler errors are build-time messages,
   not messages sent to a running applet.
*/

guides.title: 08 - What is an API?
guides.summary: An API is a set of functions that applets call to ask SIDBOX to perform tasks, such as creating a label or sending a message. The SDK declares which functions are available.
guides.notes:
The simplest way to start is with the SBOS_* convenience names shown in this Cheatsheet. Underneath, many call entries in the API table via the API pointer. Both reach the same SIDBOX services.
The API pointer is not a gadget variable. A C arrow (->) means “access a member through a pointer.”
Use F8 to find an API, read its parameters and copy its example. Do not guess function names.

guides.title: 09 - Run something repeatedly with a timer
guides.summary: A timer requests a callback at intervals. For example, a program might refresh a clock display or check whether a new message has arrived.
guides.notes:
For a GUI project, use the virtual Timer component in Designer where possible. It is not a visible button or label. Configure its interval and put the desired actions in its generated callback.
Timers are cooperative: callbacks should finish quickly rather than pause the applet for a long time. A manually created timer must be cancelled and freed when no longer needed. Designer-generated components manage their own lifecycle.

guides.title: 10 - Add a menu
guides.summary: Menus organise commands such as File, About and Quit. GUI Designer has a Menu Editor for adding titles and their individual items.
guides.notes:
1. Open the Menu Editor for the window.
2. Add a menu title such as File.
3. Add an item such as About.
4. Save/generate the .sbui.
5. Click that item in the Designer preview to navigate to its generated callback.
6. Put the desired action in that callback’s USER block.
Menus do not have to be drawn manually: the SIDBOX GUI renders the menu and handles item selection.

guides.title: 11 - Read a file from the SD card
guides.summary: Applets can read files stored on the SIDBOX SD card. A file slot is a small number used to refer to an open file.
guides.notes:
The example opens slot 0 for reading, attempts to read up to 64 bytes and then closes the slot. Check result codes before using the data.
count tells how many bytes were actually read; it may be smaller than the buffer size. Raw file data is NOT automatically a C string. The example belongs inside a function or callback and requires apis.h. File paths should match actual files on the card.

guides.title: 12 - What is inter-program messaging (IPC)?
guides.summary: IPC means Inter-Process Communication: one running applet sends a small message to another. A Messenger is a virtual gadget, meaning it has no visible control on the window.
guides.notes:
A sender chooses a receiver by applet filename, such as ipc_rx.app. A message has a type (a number chosen by the programmer) and up to 64 bytes of data. Every receiver has a mailbox holding up to 8 messages.
The receiver must be running when the sender tries to find it. If it is closed, sending can fail; this is normal. Messages are copied by SIDBOX, so two applets do not need to share memory pointers. IPC requires the V2 SDK and matching firmware.
guides.example:
/* Two running applets, for example:

   ipc_tx.app  --sends-->  ipc_rx.app

   Message type: 1
   Message text: PING

   Each applet has its own window and memory.
*/

guides.title: 13 - Receive messages using virtual Messenger
guides.summary: GUI Designer can check for incoming messages automatically. Add a Messenger to a receiving applet, enable receiving, and use its generated On Message callback.
guides.notes:
1. Create a V2 GUI project and add a Label called lbl1.
2. In the virtual components area, add a Messenger called messenger1.
3. Set Receive Enabled to Yes (the default polling interval is 25 ms).
4. Save/generate the C code.
5. Find On_messenger1_Message and put the example in its USER block.
6. Build and launch this receiver before starting the sender.
The incoming message includes sender, type, length and data. The data is a byte array, not necessarily a zero-terminated string.

guides.title: 14 - Send a message with NO handwritten IPC code
guides.summary: To make a sending applet, configure a Messenger target and connect a Button to it using Designer properties. The Button will send the configured message when clicked.
guides.notes:
1. Create a second V2 GUI project (the sender).
2. Add a virtual Messenger named messenger1.
3. Set Target applet filename to ipc_rx.app. Turn Receive Enabled off if this sender does not need to receive.
4. Add a Button. Set its visible caption to Send.
5. In the Button properties select IPC Messenger = messenger1.
6. Set IPC message type = 1 and IPC message text = PING.
7. Save/generate/build and run it beside the receiver.
Click Send. The receiver from guide 13 will display “Received 4 bytes”. Do not add a second manual send in the same Button callback or it will send twice.
guides.example:
/* Designer settings, not C to paste:
   Messenger target : ipc_rx.app
   Receive enabled  : No
   Button messenger : messenger1
   Button type      : 1
   Button text      : PING

   Designer generates the send operation.
*/

guides.title: 15 - Send and receive messages directly in C
guides.summary: Programs can also use IPC without the Designer’s automatic send action. This is useful when message content changes while an applet runs.
guides.notes:
This example belongs inside a function in a V2 applet with #include "apis.h". find() returns the current receiver instance ID, or 0 if it cannot find a unique matching applet. send() returns 0 for success; negative values indicate errors.
The receiving applet can process messages using the Messenger callback (guide 13) or the nonblocking API->ipc->receive() call. Never store a receiver ID permanently: closing and reopening the receiver creates a new ID.

guides.title: 16 - Closing an applet safely
guides.summary: Closing an applet releases its windows and owned resources. A newly opened copy of the same applet is a new instance, not a continuation of the previous one.
guides.notes:
If an applet has a Messenger mailbox, unread messages belong to the old instance and must not appear in the new one. Timers created manually should be cancelled and freed. Designer-created virtual timers and Messenger polling are managed by generated lifecycle code.
Avoid keeping pointers to another applet’s memory, and avoid placing very large arrays inside callback functions. Use the documented applet RAM/stack limits when designing bigger programs.

guides.title: 17 - GUI drawing versus graphics drawing
guides.summary: For ordinary windowed programs, add GUI gadgets in Designer. SIDBOX repaints windows and gadgets when parts of the screen change. Graphics-mode programs use a separate drawing setup.
guides.notes:
Windowed GUI applications should not casually replace global LCD or framebuffer settings. Draw into a suitable GUI gadget or follow its supported drawing callback pattern.
The example below is a graphics primitive snippet, not a complete GUI applet. It only makes sense after a graphics-mode project has configured its drawing buffer. For a first program, use Designer labels and buttons instead.

guides.title: 18 - Choosing V1 or V2
guides.summary: CoderGirl can build older V1 applets and newer V2 applets. For a new GUI project that uses Messenger, choose V2 (relocatable ARM ELF / CGARM).
guides.notes:
V1 is the original fixed-address applet format, mainly for existing programs. V2 uses relocatable applets and provides the modern per-applet execution environment.
The IPC functions documented here have been tested with V2 applets. Do not assume a V1 applet can use V2 IPC without separate compatibility support. Many standard GUI concepts apply to either format, but their build and memory models differ.
guides.example:
/* New project needing IPC?
   Project format: V2 / CGARM

   Maintaining an existing old applet?
   Keep its original V1 settings unless deliberately porting it.
*/

guides.title: 01 - V1 games vs V2 GUI applets
guides.summary: Game Designer and its platformer helpers build classic V1 fixed-address SIDBOX games. The V2/CGARM GUI Designer workflow is separate.
guides.notes:
Choose a V1 Gaming project for Game Designer, tilemaps, gfxbob_t sprites and gamehelpers. Use a V2 GUI project for windows/gadgets and relocatable GUI applets. Do not mix V1 game physics and V2 GUI startup code.
Game Designer is a visual arranger and code generator, not a separate run-time executable engine.
guides.example:
V1: Game Designer -> Generate V1 Game Code / Update Project...
V2: GUI Designer -> .sbui -> generated GUI applet.

guides.title: 02 - Explore Game Designer
guides.summary: World canvas, resource tree, camera/LCD frame, tilemaps, splines and sprite instances are edited in Game Designer.
guides.notes:
Open Game Designer in a V1 Gaming project. Add/import PPB sprites under Sprites; use the world canvas to position them. Backgrounds, sounds and palettes have their own resource categories.
The yellow 480x320 LCD frame represents the visible viewport; the world can be larger. Camera X/Y edits the current view. Right-click the world for context actions; middle-drag pans the editor.
Use Tilemap Editor... for atlas artwork and collision, Save Design for the .sbgm file.
guides.example:
Game Resources -> Sprites / Game Objects / Sounds / Backgrounds
Canvas: click/select; drag to place; right-click for actions.

guides.title: 03 - Generate, update, build
guides.summary: Generate a complete, tailored V1 starter program, with the correct SDK helpers and safe Update Project backups.
guides.notes:
1. Create a V1 Game project and a .sbgm game design. Add your tilemap, sprite named player, background and any optional objects.
2. Save Design -> Update Project... exports the required helper .c/.h files, gameassets and gamelevels, then generates maingame.c.txt.
3. The generated maingame.c.txt is now COMPLETE C source with main(), display setup, gameassets_init(), SD .map loading when chosen, tile atlas, physics, events, drawing, buffer switching and cleanup. If there is no named player/tilemap, it produces a runnable drawing starter with clear notes explaining why physics is not wired.
4. If main.c is missing, GamerGirl asks whether to create it from that generated source. Say Create main.c to get started. If main.c exists (including the generic new-project starter), the IDE NEVER overwrites it: review/copy the contents of maingame.c.txt yourself if you choose.
5. Future Update Project runs regenerate maingame.c.txt, but NEVER main.c. Changes in your main.c are yours to keep.
6. If the map is on SD, copy gamelevels/level1.map and the matching atlas PPB to their expected SD locations; music/sounds remain SD resources. Build the V1 game normally.
7. Existing gamehelpers .c/.h sources are updated from the SDK with a dated ZIP backup before any writes. Do not permanently customise generated outputs.
guides.example:
Save Design -> Update Project...
Open maingame.c.txt -> whole working program for YOUR design
Missing main.c? -> Create main.c (optional)
Existing main.c? -> untouched; copy/adapt explicitly if desired

guides.title: 04 - World positions vs screen positions
guides.summary: Physics and collision use world coordinates; the renderer subtracts the camera position when drawing.
guides.notes:
The 480x320 LCD is a window onto a possibly larger level. A sprite placed at world X=800 does not collide at its on-screen X coordinate. Use physics.x100 / 100 and physics.y100 / 100 (or the generated game loop values) for collection/collision.
A placed game object uses its own canvas world coordinates and can optionally follow a spline. Avoid subtracting camera X/Y yourself when using the generated world-object draw function.
guides.example:
gameworlditems_draw(camera_x, camera_y);
/* Object collision uses WORLD positions, not camera-adjusted screen positions. */

guides.title: 01 - Advanced Platformer overview
guides.summary: V1 Advanced Platformer currently provides tilemap collision, player physics, collectables, keys, switches, doors, moving lifts, conveyors, springs, splines, animations and sound events.
guides.notes:
This section documents the REAL controls in the current Game Designer. A game object starts as a PPB sprite INSTANCE, then gains gameplay behaviour in Game Object Properties.
You can assemble puzzles (key -> door), moving hazards/platforms, secret pressure plates, launchers and sliding jumps. The game still owns its overall loop and any custom logic such as score/health.
Change an option, Save Design, use Update Project..., then test on SIDBOX.
guides.example:
Example puzzle: Key [Disable target] -> Door / Solid blocker
Example traversal: Touch spring [launch right + slidy] -> moving lift

guides.title: 02 - Tilemaps, walls, slopes and hazards
guides.summary: Tilemap Editor stores artwork separately from collision: floors, walls, slopes, one-way surfaces, hazards and door-marked tiles.
guides.notes:
Open Tilemap Editor... and edit/export the level. The graphics map uses 16-bit IDs; collision uses separate 8-bit IDs. The helper resolves normal terrain collisions. Hazard/door tile meanings require your game logic where indicated by the tilemap helper.
The generated level references a PPB atlas on the SD card, loaded once with a size/checksum check. Do not assume the C level embeds atlas pixels. Copy the CURRENT atlas to SD.
VERY IMPORTANT: A switch-controlled Door / Solid blocker must not overlap permanently solid tilemap collision, or the invisible solid tile remains after disabling the door.
See gamehelpers/gametilemap.txt in your game project for rendering and atlas-lifetime details.
guides.example:
Tilemap Editor... -> Export Tilemap -> Update Project...
Startup: game_level1_load_atlas() after gameassets_init()
Shutdown: game_level1_unload_atlas() before gameassets_shutdown()

guides.title: 03 - Player physics and frame order
guides.summary: The advanced tilemap player helper handles jumping, gravity, collisions and slopes. World objects must update before and after player physics in the proper order.
guides.notes:
Use the actual project-generated maingame.c.txt as the source of truth for your level and includes. Player physics runs once per VBlank. Normal jumps retain variable height (short release, long hold); springs use a separate fixed launch arc unless intentional extra jump boost is enabled.
The generated world-player bindings connect physics position, vertical velocity, on-ground and optional jump state. Do not mix the basic platformer and tilemap physics controllers on one player.
Ordering is essential for carrying, spring launch, doors and button switches.

guides.title: 04 - Sprites and Game Objects are two views
guides.summary: A configured Game Object is still a sprite. Selecting it on the canvas reveals its Game Objects tree alias; the same instance remains under Sprites.
guides.notes:
Sprites holds the artwork placement and image reference. Game Objects holds the behaviour of configured sprites; they are not two separate copies.
Click an ordinary sprite on the world canvas and Sprites is highlighted. Click a configured object and Game Objects is highlighted. You can also select its Sprites entry to edit ordinary sprite properties.
Right-click a sprite or its tree entry and select Configure Game Object... to assign behaviour. Its stable instance ID makes links resistant to renaming/reordering.
guides.example:
Game Resources -> Sprites -> [your sprite]
Game Resources -> Game Objects -> [same configured sprite]
Right-click -> Configure Game Object...

guides.title: 05 - Hitboxes and activation state
guides.summary: Game-object behaviours use a configurable rectangular collision width and height, plus an Active when the level starts option.
guides.notes:
For an object to have gameplay behaviour, it must reference a PPB sprite at 100% scale. Adjust Collision width / height to fit the intended touch or solid area, not necessarily the image size. Game Designer displays a dashed hitbox outline for configured objects.
Active when the level starts OFF is useful for hidden/unlocked later objects; a trigger or key can Enable one. A disabled object is not drawn or processed as an active collision target.
An ordinary Decoration has no special gameplay behaviour.
Editing artwork is separate from configuring one placed instance.
guides.example:
Configure Game Object...
Behaviour: Door / Solid blocker
Collision width: 24   Collision height: 48
Active when the level starts: ON

guides.title: 06 - Collectables: coins, health, gems and keys
guides.summary: Collectable supports Coin, Health, Key and Gem pickup types, a numeric value, optional animation/spline, pickup sound and respawn timing.
guides.notes:
Add a PPB sprite (100% scale), Configure Game Object... -> Collectable. Choose Pickup type and Pickup value. Use Respawn after frames = 0 for a permanent pickup or a positive number for a timed respawn.
The generated gameworlditems_check(...) performs player-bound collision after movement. Your game callback determines score/health/gameplay rewards for ordinary pickups; do not assume selecting Health edits your player-health variable automatically.
A Key can additionally perform a linked Enable/Disable/Toggle action, detailed below. Sound effects are optional.
guides.example:
Behaviour: Collectable
Pickup type: Coin / Health / Key / Gem
Pickup value: 10
Respawn after frames: 0 (never)

guides.title: 07 - Walkthrough: key unlocks a door
guides.summary: Use a Key collectable to Disable a placed Door / Solid blocker elsewhere in the level. No manually typed numeric IDs are needed.
guides.notes:
1. Place a PPB sprite for the door at 100% scale. Configure its Behaviour as Door / Solid blocker; size its collision rectangle and leave Active when the level starts checked.
2. Place a second PPB sprite for the key at 100%. Configure as Collectable -> Key.
3. In the KEY properties, set Activate/deactivate object to your door sprite and Linked action to Disable target.
4. Set key Respawn after frames to 0 if it should be collected once.
5. Save Design and Update Project... to regenerate the binding. Collecting the key deactivates the door (both appearance and blocking).
Do not paint permanently solid map tiles in the openable doorway.
guides.example:
DOOR: Behaviour = Door / Solid blocker; Active at start = ON
KEY: Behaviour = Collectable; Pickup type = Key
     Activate/deactivate object = [door]
     Linked action = Disable target
     Respawn after frames = 0

guides.title: 08 - Doors and solid blockers
guides.summary: A Door / Solid blocker is a full-solid rectangular runtime object. Disabling it also removes its live solid collision.
guides.notes:
Configure a sprite as Door / Solid blocker, size its hitbox, and choose its startup active state. A key or switch can Enable, Disable or Toggle it. An active door blocks player movement; a disabled door is hidden/non-blocking.
Use Active at start OFF + Enable target for a barrier that appears later, or ON + Disable target for an unlockable door. Unlike a normal lift, the door is solid rather than a one-way platform.
Do not leave permanent solid tilemap collision inside its doorway. For unusually high speeds or moving blockers, test collision on real hardware.
guides.example:
Start ON + Disable target  = unlocked/opened door
Start OFF + Enable target  = new barrier appears
Start ON + Toggle target   = open/close switch

guides.title: 09 - Switches: touch or FIRE2
guides.summary: Trigger / Switch controls another placed object with Enable, Disable or Toggle. It can activate on contact or require FIRE2 while touching.
guides.notes:
1. Configure a PPB sprite as Trigger / Switch. Set its Collision width / height as a sensor region.
2. Select Activate/deactivate object; choose Linked action.
3. Leave Require FIRE2 while touching unchecked for a touch plate. Check it for a deliberate button-activated switch (FIRE2 is the second fire button, not the normal Jump FIRE).
4. For a repeatable switch, leave Remove switch after activation OFF. It rearms after a new touch, or a new FIRE2 press while touching. Holding contact does not toggle the door each frame.
5. Save Design -> Update Project.... The existing gameworlditems_after() call handles switches in the normal generated game loop.
guides.example:
Behaviour: Trigger / Switch
Activate/deactivate object: [door]
Linked action: Toggle target (ON / OFF)
Require FIRE2 while touching: ON
Remove switch after activation: OFF

guides.title: 10 - One-shot triggers and room discovery
guides.summary: A trigger can perform its linked action once and remove itself. Useful for secrets, opening another room, and single-use pressure plates.
guides.notes:
Configure Trigger / Switch with the desired target/action, then check Remove switch after activation (one-shot). With FIRE2 unchecked, entering its hitbox activates it. Afterwards that trigger is disabled and no longer displayed/processed.
Set the TARGET initially inactive and use Enable for a hidden item or passage that appears after entering a room. Set target initially active and choose Disable to open an already-closed barrier.
This is an in-level action, not an automatic persistent save to SD. Keeping a door unlocked across game restarts requires your game save logic.
guides.example:
INVISIBLE/DECORATED SENSOR: Trigger / Switch
Target: [remote door]   Linked action: Disable target
Require FIRE2: OFF      Remove after activation: ON

guides.title: 11 - Springers: normal bounce
guides.summary: Spring / Bouncer launches the player upward when landing on top. Its upward strength and extra-jump option are independently configurable.
guides.notes:
Configure a PPB sprite as Spring / Bouncer. Spring upward launch is measured in pixels per frame. The normal mode triggers only on a landing from above.
A spring normally overrides the regular jump impulse and uses the controlled shorter spring arc; HOLDING Jump does not secretly add extra height. Combine jump + spring launch is an explicit optional boost when a NEW Jump press coincides with contact (requires jump physics bindings).
Set Spring sideways launch to zero for a purely vertical bounce. Each successful bounce may play its configured launch sound.
guides.example:
Behaviour: Spring / Bouncer
Spring upward launch (px/frame): 11
Spring sideways launch: 0
Activate on touch (any side): OFF
Combine jump + spring launch: OFF

guides.title: 12 - Springers: touch and directional launches
guides.summary: A spring can trigger when touched from ANY side and launch left, right or vertically, without requiring a landing from above.
guides.notes:
Enable Activate on touch (any side). Contact from above, below, left or right triggers the spring once; the player must leave the hitbox before it can rearm.
Spring sideways launch: negative launches LEFT, positive launches RIGHT, zero is vertical. This is independent of the upward strength and of Slidy kickback.
You can build bumper walls, sideways cannons, or ceiling springs. Use modest initial strengths and a correctly sized hitbox; very large values can send the player through nearby scenery between frames.
guides.example:
SPRING A: Upward 11, Sideways -6, Touch ON  -> up and LEFT
SPRING B: Upward 11, Sideways +6, Touch ON  -> up and RIGHT
SPRING C: Upward 11, Sideways  0, Touch OFF -> land to bounce

guides.title: 13 - Springers: slidy inertia and jump boost
guides.summary: Slidy kickback applies decaying horizontal momentum after a spring launch, including a ground skid; the old rigid kickback is still available.
guides.notes:
Slidy kickback OFF: the sideways launch stays constant until landing, then stops.
Slidy kickback ON: the initial sideways impulse gradually loses speed in the air and has stronger friction on the ground. Steering still works; walls stop the slide. The spring sideways launch value controls direction and initial kick.
The added Combine jump + spring launch setting is SEPARATE and should usually stay OFF until you intentionally want a stronger spring. Existing projects default the newer options OFF.
This mode is per spring, so normal springs and slidy springs can coexist.
guides.example:
Behaviour: Spring / Bouncer
Spring sideways launch: +8
Activate on touch (any side): ON
Slidy kickback (inertia + friction): ON
Combine jump + spring launch: OFF

guides.title: 14 - Moving lifts and platforms
guides.summary: Moving platform / Lift can carry the player on its top while travelling along a configured spline path.
guides.notes:
Place a platform sprite and configure as Moving platform / Lift. Assign Movement spline if it should travel; otherwise it remains at its placed coordinates.
The generated helper handles swept landings and attempts to carry the player without embedding them in solid tilemap walls or slope interiors (when an attached collision map exists). Sideways carry stops at a wall even if the platform continues beneath the rider.
Lift surfaces are one-way from above; they are not solid ceilings or general vertical walls. Optional sound events cover movement start/move/stop/reversal.
guides.example:
Behaviour: Moving platform / Lift
Movement spline: [lift_path]
Collision width/height: fit the platform top
Optional sound: Start / Move / Stop / Reverse

guides.title: 15 - Conveyors
guides.summary: Conveyor platforms move the player sideways while they stand on top, with a signed speed and optional ambient audio.
guides.notes:
Configure the sprite as Conveyor, adjust Collision width/height and Conveyor px/frame. Negative values move LEFT, positive values move RIGHT. As with lifts, it acts from the top rather than as a solid wall.
A conveyor can also be attached to a Movement spline for a travelling belt. Test interaction near walls and platform edges. The ambient sound can be given a radius and fading controls.
guides.example:
Behaviour: Conveyor
Conveyor px/frame: -2 (left) / +2 (right)
Movement spline: None or [path]
Ambient sound: optional

guides.title: 16 - Splines: move objects through a level
guides.summary: A spline is a set of editor control points used to move sprites/objects along a path; optional pauses can be placed at nodes.
guides.notes:
Create/edit a path in Game Designer (at least two nodes). Configure a placed sprite as a Game Object (for example Moving platform / Lift), then set Game Object Properties -> Movement spline to that path. Choose Update Game Project. GamerGirl installs gamespline.c/.h and exports splinepaths.c/.h, then generates gameworlditems.c and a COMPLETE maingame.c.txt.

For attached objects, main.c only needs gameworlditems_init(), gameworlditems_update(1), and gameworlditems_draw(camera_x,camera_y), already emitted by the starter. NEVER call start_spline()/run_spline() a second time for the same object. Normal sprite/decoration resources aren't automatically attached, even if a spline exists.

For manual spline movement on an ordinary sprite, see the full copyable example emitted into maingame.c.txt when your design contains spline paths. Make sure gamespline.c and splinepaths.c are part of the compiled project, and do not draw the same sprite twice. The IDE never overwrites your existing main.c.

guides.title: 17 - Sprite animation on objects
guides.summary: Game objects can animate frames from a PPB atlas while their behaviour (pickup, spring, platform, etc.) continues running.
guides.notes:
Tick Animate sprite frames. Configure First frame (0 based), Number of frames and Frames per picture. Modes are Loop, Ping-pong, or Once. A sprite can animate and move along a spline simultaneously.
Keep sprite sheet dimensions/cell layout consistent with the actual PPB. The generic Sprite Animation helper can also be used in hand-written game C.
guides.example:
Animate sprite frames: ON
First frame: 0  Number of frames: 4
Frames per picture: 5
Animation mode: Loop

guides.title: 18 - Tile atlas animation
guides.summary: Tilemap graphics IDs and atlas tile animations are managed separately from placed Game Object sprite animation.
guides.notes:
Open Tilemap Editor... to set animation sequences in the tile atlas. The runtime advances shared atlas animation by graphics ID with game_tilemap_animation_tick(1) per VBlank. There is no need to add a world object for every animated tile.
The atlas PPB on SD must be the same current artwork that the generated level validates. Regenerate/export the level and update SD assets after editing atlas graphics.
guides.example:
game_tilemap_animation_tick(1); // once per VBlank
/* Then blit the visible tiles with game_tilemap_blit_view(...). */

guides.title: 19 - Sound effects, radius and channels
guides.summary: Game Object Properties can link existing Sound resources to pickup, respawn, lift, conveyor and spring events.
guides.notes:
Add/import WAV sounds under Sounds, configure the SIDBOX audio channel, and select those resources in the Game Object Properties sound section. Events are generated automatically for the supported object type.
Optional Audio radius and fade frames help with spatial effects for applicable sounds. Shared channels interrupt/reconfigure one another, so choose channels deliberately. Triggerable links have no dedicated switch sound field in the current dialog; add a separate sound event in your game code if needed.
guides.example:
Game Resources -> Sounds -> [WAV sound]
Game Object Properties -> SOUND / AUDIO -> choose event sound
Update Project... -> regenerated event wrappers

guides.title: 20 - Troubleshooting checklist
guides.summary: Use these checks when a door does not unlock, a spring will not bounce, or generated game behaviour seems missing.
guides.notes:
1. Did you Save Design, then Update Project... after changing behaviour?
2. Is the sprite a real PPB at 100% scale, not a placeholder or background?
3. Does the object hitbox overlap the player path?
4. Is the target a configured game object, selected in the dropdown? A deleted target will produce a generation error.
5. Is the target initially active/inactive as the action expects?
6. Is the door ALSO painted as permanent solid tilemap collision? Remove that collision from its opening.
7. Does main.c follow maingame.c.txt, including before -> physics -> after, pickup checks and draw?
8. Is the latest tile atlas PPB copied to SD, and loaded at startup?
9. Are you using Jump/FIRE versus FIRE2 as intended?
10. Avoid hand-editing generated gameworlditems.c; change the .sbgm design and regenerate.
guides.example:
A key unlock did nothing?
Check: Key -> target = correct Door -> Linked action = Disable
Check: door start active ON, no permanent solid tile in opening
Check: gameworlditems_check(...) runs after player movement.

guides.title: 21 - Puzzle recipes to try
guides.summary: Combine documented features without any new engine code: secret doors, timed pickups, moving springs, reversible switches and sliding traversal puzzles.
guides.notes:
Secret exit: a one-shot touch trigger disables a remote door.
Wall switch: a repeatable FIRE2 Trigger / Switch toggles a door each press.
Hidden treasure: a key enables an initially inactive Gem collectable.
Timed coin trail: moving/animated collectables with a respawn delay.
Spring gauntlet: touch springs with opposite left/right horizontal launches and Slidy ON.
Elevator puzzle: moving lift on a spline carries the player up to a key which disables a door.
Remember: target actions affect objects in the current running level; persistent state across reloads is not automatically saved.
guides.example:
Trigger -> [Door] Disable + one-shot ON
Key -> [Gem] Enable (Gem initially inactive)
Spring -> sideways +8, Touch ON, Slidy ON

guides.title: 22 - Switches that start or stop music
guides.summary: Trigger / Switch game objects can automatically start a tune from Game Resources > Music or stop the active music when touched or activated with FIRE2.
guides.notes:
1. Add a tracker tune in the Music branch; keep the actual audio file on the SD card at its game resource path.
2. Select a placed sprite, right-click and choose Configure Game Object, then set Trigger / Switch.
3. Under When triggered — music, choose Play selected tune and select the Music tree resource in Tune. To stop the current song instead, choose Stop current music; no Tune selection is needed.
4. Choose touch or Require FIRE2; choose Remove switch after activation for a one-time zone.
5. Update Game Project to regenerate gameworlditems.c and gameassets.c. The game loop must call music_update() regularly (the generated main example does).
6. Music and an Enable/Disable/Toggle linked-object action may be configured on the same switch.
Music is global SIDBOX playback; starting a track replaces the song already playing, and Stop stops the currently playing tune. The source Music resource is referenced by a stable ID, not a hard-coded filename. Existing game main.c is never overwritten.

guides.title: 23 - Export embedded C or SD .map tilemaps
guides.summary: Save level tile graphics, collisions and tile animations inside the .app as generated .c, or export a compact checked .map file loaded from the SD card.
guides.notes:
1. In Game Designer open the tilemap context menu and choose Export Tilemap (.c / .map)...
2. Choose Export embedded .c to compile data into the game, or Export SD .map to write gamelevels/level1.map alongside the tiny generated level1.c/.h wrapper.
3. The choice is saved in the .sbgm game design and respected by Update Game Project. Earlier designs default to embedded C.
4. In SD mode copy gamelevels/level1.map onto the SIDBOX SD card at gamelevels/level1.map. AFTER initMalloc() and gameassets_init(), call game_level1_load_map("gamelevels/level1.map") and test its return value, THEN call game_level1_load_atlas().
5. When leaving a level, first game_level1_unload_atlas(), then game_level1_unload_map(), then gameassets_shutdown().
6. The loader checks magic, version, dimensions, tile size, tile IDs, collision IDs, tile animations and checksum before replacing live data. It leaves the current map intact on failure. You can call it again to load another compatible .map using the same tile size and atlas.
IMPORTANT: .map only includes tile graphics, tile collisions, and tile animations. Objects, sprites, keys, door states, positions, and music triggers are still compiled from the current Game Designer layout; this is not yet a complete multi-level object loader. The atlas PPB is a separate SD file. Keep gamehelpers/gametilemap.c/.h updated with Update Project.

guides.title: 24 - Hazard tiles: Entered, Inside, Exited
guides.summary: Tile hazards are non-blocking sensors: receive ENTERED on contact, INSIDE each following physics update, and EXITED when leaving.
guides.notes:
1. Paint GAME_TILE_HAZARD (collision type 5) in the Tilemap Editor. Tiles remain non-blocking.
2. Register game_death_set_callback(on_player_death, NULL) after game_tile_player_start(); the four-argument callback signature does not change.
3. GAME_HAZARD_TILE_ENTERED fires on the first overlapping frame, GAME_HAZARD_TILE_INSIDE on each later physics update while overlapping, GAME_HAZARD_TILE_EXITED on the first update after leaving. Crossing adjacent hazard tiles does not create false exits. Fast swept crossings still generate ENTERED.
4. At 50 FPS, INSIDE can occur around 50 times per second; DO NOT subtract an entire hit point every callback unless intended. Throttle with a counter or use game time.
5. Existing GAME_DEATH_TILE_HAZARD equals GAME_HAZARD_TILE_ENTERED, so old callbacks retain one-hit-on-entry behaviour. GAME_DEATH_ZONE likewise equals GAME_HAZARD_ZONE_ENTERED.
6. Touching a hazard NEVER freezes physics by itself. Your own callback may call game_death_mark_dead() when health reaches zero. game_tile_player_reset() rearms player physics.
7. A death triggered separately by game_death_trigger(GAME_DEATH_SCRIPT, x, y) still fires GAME_DEATH_SCRIPT once and freezes the player.
8. Update Game Project to replace gametilemap.c/.h and generated gameworlditems.c. No edits to current main.c are necessary unless you want to respond to the new events.

guides.title: 25 - Hazard Zones: Three contact events
guides.summary: A Game Object Hazard Zone reports entered, inside, and exited through the same callback, without blocking or automatically killing the player.
guides.notes:
1. Right-click a sprite -> Configure Game Object -> Hazard Zone (touch = callback). Saved Death Zone objects remain compatible.
2. Give it a hitbox and enable it. It is a SENSOR, not a wall.
3. gameworlditems_after() dispatches GAME_HAZARD_ZONE_ENTERED at first overlap, GAME_HAZARD_ZONE_INSIDE each subsequent overlapping call, and GAME_HAZARD_ZONE_EXITED after leaving all active Hazard Zones. Moving between overlapping/adjacent zones is treated as continued contact.
4. Your existing callback game_death_set_callback(on_player_death, NULL) is unchanged. Old GAME_DEATH_ZONE comparisons still match ENTERED.
5. INSIDE is per call to gameworlditems_after(), usually once per game frame; throttle damage according to your game update rate. If tile hazards and zones overlap, both may send events in a frame.
6. Only your game can call game_death_mark_dead() to freeze physics. Call game_tile_player_reset() to respawn. Explicit scripted death still uses game_death_trigger(GAME_DEATH_SCRIPT, x, y).
7. Update Game Project to regenerate gameworlditems.c after rebuilding this IDE.

guides.title: 26 - Stamp Bank: Reusable tile arrangements
guides.summary: Build named multi-tile stamps in the Tilemap Editor and paint them onto the map as normal cells, preserving each cell's graphic and collision.
guides.notes:
1. Open Game Designer -> Tilemap Editor. On the RIGHT, Stamp Bank is above Stamp Editor; the tile atlas remains on the LEFT.
2. Click Add to create a stamp. Rename it and set Width/Height (1-16 cells). The lower-right editor displays the stamp grid.
3. Click an atlas graphic on the LEFT, then LEFT-click a cell in the lower-right Stamp Editor to assign that graphic. The toolbar Paint collision option can also assign per-cell collision types. RIGHT-click clears both layers of a stamp cell.
4. Click the stamp thumbnail in the upper-right bank. Your canvas brush becomes that entire stamp. LEFT-drag places it on a stamp-sized grid anchored to your first click; RIGHT-drag clears its whole footprint on the same grid. Fast drags fill intervening stamp positions. Map edges clip safely.
5. To resume painting ordinary tiles, click an atlas tile on the LEFT. The stamp remains editable in the lower-right panel.
6. Stamps are saved with the .sbgm design (including names, dimensions and cell data), and edits/placements use Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y. Removing a stamp never removes cells already painted onto the map.
7. The exported .c/.map contains only the ordinary placed tile IDs, collisions and flip flags; there is NO stamp data at runtime. Original projects without stamps load normally.
8. Individual stamp cells preserve their own X/Y flip flags. Mirror stamp X/Y reverses positions and XORs those flags during painting.
9. Stamps are tied to the tile size used when they were made. Switch the map back to that tile size to place the stamp.
guides.example:
Stamp Bank -> Add -> Rename -> Width 4, Height 4
Click tile in atlas -> click cell in Stamp Editor
Click stamp thumbnail -> click or drag in map
Save (stays open and saves .sbgm), or Apply to Design (closes)

guides.title: 27 - Complete beginner: first playable V1 platformer
guides.summary: Create a scrolling, playable V1 game with a tilemap and player, using the generated complete starter program.
guides.notes:
1. Create a V1 Gaming project (the IDE initially supplies a generic main.c).
2. Open Game Designer, add a tilemap and select its PPB atlas. Paint floor graphics and SOLID collision tiles.
3. Add an ordinary PPB sprite named player (the name is case-insensitive); place it above a solid floor. Add a background resource if desired.
4. Save Design, then Update Project... This exports the tilemap and helper code and writes a COMPLETE, project-specific maingame.c.txt.
5. Open maingame.c.txt in the project tree. The text is valid C, with includes, graphics mode, asset and atlas loading, player physics, double buffering, map drawing, and optional object/callback logic.
6. Existing main.c is NOT overwritten. For a new project, back up your generic main.c yourself and copy the full generated example into it to start playing. If main.c was deleted or missing, an optional Create main.c prompt appears automatically.
7. If using SD .map export, copy gamelevels/level1.map and the matching atlas PPB onto the card; also copy any PPB, WAV and music assets that are loaded from SD.
8. Build and run on SIDBOX. With a map and player, getjoyport() controls the player; camera follows the player. Configured doors, springs and pickups run through gameworlditems.
9. Add your game rules to main.c; regenerate helpers freely afterwards because GamerGirl does not modify main.c.
Remember: the generated example cannot invent a physics character when no sprite is named player, and Qt IDE compile/hardware still need checking on your system.
guides.example:
Game Designer -> Tilemap Editor -> paint solid floor
Game Resources -> Sprites -> PPB sprite named player
Save Design -> Update Project
Open maingame.c.txt -> copy entire file into your own main.c
Build the V1 game

guides.title: 28 - Flip X/Y for individual tile cells
guides.summary: Mirror tile graphics independently without duplicating 8x8 atlas artwork.
guides.notes:
1. Open GamerGirl Tilemap Editor. Click an atlas graphic on the left.
2. Enable Cell Flip X and/or Cell Flip Y in the paint toolbar.
3. Click the map to paint with the chosen graphic and flip flags; preview and game output should match.
4. To flip an ALREADY PLACED tile without changing its graphic ID, select Paint graphic: Don't change graphic. Keep Apply flip flags and paint the chosen cell using the checkboxes.
5. For collision-only edits, set Don't change flip flags and Don't change graphic.
6. The separate collision tile remains unchanged when merely flipping artwork. If using directional slopes, confirm that the collision geometry still matches the artwork.
7. Update Game Project after regenerating the level. Embedded .c exports a new game_level1_flips[] array; external .map exports SBMP v2 with per-cell flips. Copy the updated SD map and helper files.
8. Existing .sbgm projects and SBMP v1 maps default to no flips. The new helper accepts both v1 and v2; the old helper cannot load v2.

guides.title: 29 - Mirror stamps while keeping per-cell flips
guides.summary: Mirror whole stamp placements while preserving constituent cell transformations.
guides.notes:
1. Create/select a stamp in the right-hand Stamp Bank. Select atlas graphics and paint in the lower-right Stamp Editor.
2. Set Cell Flip X and/or Y before painting individual stamp cells. Each retains its own flip flags when saved, reopened, or resized.
3. Select the stamp thumbnail as your map brush. Enable Mirror stamp X or Mirror stamp Y in the toolbar.
4. When placing the stamp, the editor reverses the cell positions along each chosen axis and XORs the corresponding flip flags. Double mirroring restores the original orientation.
5. The source stamp itself is not changed; mirror controls affect the placement only. Previously placed stamps are ordinary map cells, and retain the flags from the moment they were placed.
6. Horizontal mirroring of a complete stamp swaps the two slope collision IDs (rising/falling). Vertical mirroring only affects graphics because ceiling slopes are not currently supported.
7. Use Save to commit the stamp bank and painted map without closing the tile editor, or Apply to Design to close it. Regenerate your map export and project helpers for SIDBOX.

guides.title: 30 - Save while editing and drag stamps on a stamp-sized grid
guides.summary: Save map and stamp edits without closing the editor, and paint repeating stamps aligned to the first mouse click.
guides.notes:
1. At the bottom of Tilemap Editor, Save commits your current tiles and stamp definitions to the Game Designer AND saves the .sbgm file without closing the editor. You can continue painting immediately.
2. Save offers the existing export choice: Yes saves the design and exports the level/required files, No saves only the game design.
3. Apply to Design retains its previous behaviour: closes the editor and prompts about exporting. Choosing No applies changes to the parent design in memory, which you can save later.
4. Cancel discards edits since the most recent successful Save or Apply, but cannot undo an earlier successful disk Save.
5. Select a stamp in the upper-right Stamp Bank. Press and hold LEFT on the map: the FIRST clicked cell anchors a temporary grid with spacing equal to stamp width and height. Move the mouse to tile the stamp without overlaps.
6. Moving quickly across cells fills intervening stamp positions. Left/up movement also snaps correctly. RIGHT-drag erases whole stamps on the same grid. Releasing the mouse ends the grid; the next stroke gets a fresh anchor.
7. Single atlas tiles still paint at the normal cell resolution. Individual stamp cells retain graphics, collision types and X/Y flips; Mirror stamp X/Y still works. Ctrl+Z undoes a full dragged stamp stroke as one operation.
8. Stamps are purely design-time. Neither the embedded .c nor the SD .map file format changes for stamp-sized dragging.
guides.example:
Stamp Bank -> choose 4x2 stamp -> click map at cell (7,5)
Drag right: origins (7,5), (11,5), (15,5), ...
Drag down: origins (7,7), (7,9), ...
Save -> continue editing, Apply to Design -> close editor, Cancel -> discard unsaved changes

guides.title: 31 - Live tile and stamp placement preview
guides.summary: Hover over the tilemap before painting to see a transparent preview of the selected cell or whole stamp, including mirroring and individual flip flags.
guides.notes:
1. Select a tile in the atlas on the left, or select a stamp from the right-hand Stamp Bank.
2. Move the mouse over the central tilemap. The tile or full stamp appears as a semi-transparent graphic with a bright square outline before you click.
3. Cell Flip X/Y, Mirror Stamp X/Y, and the individual flips already saved in the stamp are included in the preview.
4. When dragging a stamp, the preview snaps to the temporary stamp-sized grid anchored by your first click. Release the mouse to reset the grid.
5. Right-dragging shows a red erase outline. Moving the cursor outside the canvas hides the preview.
6. In the lower-right Stamp Editor, the selected atlas tile also appears over the cell you are about to paint.
7. Preview does not edit or export anything. Only actual brush strokes change the tilemap.
guides.example: For an 8x8 cell map, a 4x2 stamp displays an 32x16 pixel translucent preview. Click-and-drag to place complete stamps with the same flip flags you see in the preview.

guides.title: 32 - Collision stamps: Editable point-defined slopes
guides.summary: Create point-defined ground surfaces over faded tile artwork; reused slope shapes are linked to whole stamp placements and exported compactly.
guides.notes:
1. Under Tile Stamps select the matching artwork for the faint reference. Switch to Collision Stamps and Add a shape.
2. A new shape starts with two endpoints on opposite edges. LEFT-CLICK open space to insert a point; drag any point to move it; RIGHT-CLICK an interior point to delete it. Endpoints can move vertically but remain on the left and right boundaries.
3. Use the stamp bank to select a slope; the point editor, name, dimensions and brush NOW all switch to the chosen shape. SHIFT+LEFT-CLICK an already-placed slope on the tilemap to open its shared definition directly. Select a point with a click or drag it; precise Point X/Y spinboxes also move the selected point. Use Insert Point to split the widest segment, and Delete Point to remove a selected interior point. Endpoints are locked to left/right edges but their Y may change.
4. Select the shape thumbnail. LEFT-DRAG on the map to place whole collision instances on a stamp-sized temporary grid. Mirror stamp X flips the slope without altering the shared definition. RIGHT-CLICK/DRAG on an occupied region removes the ENTIRE instance; overlaps replace whole previous instances.
5. Editing the original shape points changes every placement of that shape in the level immediately (including mirrored copies). Width/Height changes also update placed copies if the new footprints fit on the map and do not overlap other stamps or collisions. Invalid resizing is rejected without changing the original. Collisions remain separate from graphics and tile flip flags. Graphical stamps can overwrite collision placements; apply collision stamps last.
6. After Save / Update Game Project, the generated helper automatically handles collisions. Pure point-slope maps use SD SBMP v4 with a compact per-cell reference map and shape/placement tables. No per-pixel height array is exported for NEW slope shapes. Embedded C exports the same tables.
7. Old Stage 3.35 painted slopes (collision type 7) remain exact legacy per-pixel data, because they did not record original stamp identities. Mixed v4 maps include the legacy heights until old slopes are cleared or repainted.
8. Update the gametilemap.c/.h helpers when the IDE prompts, rebuild the .app, and recopy level1.map to SD. The v4 loader still accepts old v1/v2/v3 files.
9. This remains walkable ground with solid space below the surface only. Very steep faces may behave as walls. No ceilings/loops or vertical mirroring.
guides.example: Collision Stamps -> select a slope thumbnail OR Shift+left-click a placed slope -> edit points by dragging or entering X/Y -> every placed copy redraws instantly. Save -> Update Game Project -> rebuild and recopy the SD .map to see the changed collisions on SIDBOX.

guides.title: 33 - Whole collision stamps and compact slope maps
guides.summary: Edit shared polyline slopes, mirror placements and delete them as whole objects without leaving stray collision cells.
guides.notes: Create/edit points in Collision Stamps. Placing stores an instance, not a copied array of heights. Right-drag across a placed slope removes it entirely. Changing the original points updates all its instances. Rebuild the game after Update Project, and copy the new v4 .map onto SD. Existing v3 height-painted areas are kept for compatibility, but need repainting as point-defined stamps to remove their original dense array from exports. Graphical stamps still edit collision cells and may replace point-defined placements where painted. Keep the collision-only pass last. Shift+left-click any placed slope to select and edit its shared source. Editing points updates all copies immediately inside the IDE. Safe resizing updates every placement, or declines if it would overlap other collisions or exceed map bounds.
guides.example: Shift+left-click a placed slope -> select a point in the lower editor -> drag it or set exact X/Y -> every copy updates. Insert Point / Delete Point work on the shared definition; Ctrl+Z restores the prior points.

guides.title: 34 - Tilemap editor view and brush memory
guides.summary: Keep zoom, brush choices and per-project pan positions between Tilemap Editor sessions.
guides.notes: Zoom, collision brush, selected graphic ID, graphic paint mode, and X/Y/front brush flags are restored when reopening. Map panning is remembered separately for each game-design directory. Save or close the editor to store the view. The atlas on the left reflows its tile IDs to the panel width: scroll vertically to reach every atlas cell.
guides.example: Zoom to 3x, select atlas tile 42 and Collision=Dont change, pan to a hill, then Apply and reopen: the view and brushes return.

guides.title: 35 - Draw tiles in front of the player
guides.summary: Put foliage, arches and platforms over the player without a second tilemap or larger SD file.
guides.notes: In the Tilemap Editor choose Apply tile flags and check Draw in front of player, then paint individual tiles. For graphical stamp placement, check Stamp: use Draw Front setting to make the whole stamp use that checkbox for front/back; otherwise, every stamp cell uses its saved front/back flag. In either case, per-cell X/Y flips and stamp mirroring are retained. The front bit shares the existing per-cell flag byte with Flip X/Y. The main rendering pass skips these tiles; a second pass draws ONLY front tiles after sprites and player. Collision settings are independent. Old maps and embedded C maps remain valid. Projects with older gametilemap helpers are offered a backed-up update. Re-export the level after editing, then rebuild the .app; SD map version remains unchanged. Existing hand-written main.c needs the call after drawing the player.

guides.title: 36 - Copy and paste a tilemap region
guides.summary: Shift-drag a rectangular map area and use it immediately as a temporary stamp with graphics, collisions and flip/foreground flags.
guides.notes: Shift+left-drag in the main map selects an inclusive rectangle. A simple Shift-click still opens a placed point-slope for editing. After selecting, move the cursor to preview the copied area; left-click pastes once, and left-drag repositions the preview without pasting until you click. Right-click erases the whole temporary brush footprint. Press Escape to discard the temporary brush and leave paste mode WITHOUT making any final paste; Shift+Escape is not required. Already-pasted changes remain and can be undone with Ctrl+Z. All graphics, X/Y and draw-front flags, ordinary collisions and legacy slope samples are copied. Point-based collision stamps keep their shared definitions: selecting part of one expands the copy to include its entire placement. Stamp: use Draw Front setting optionally overrides the copied foreground bits when placing. The temporary copy is never added to the permanent stamp bank. Every paste/erase is a single undo action. Areas must fit fully in the map; nothing is exported or saved until a paste or erase is applied. Save or Apply to Design saves the edited map normally.
guides.example: Shift+drag over a 4x2-cell platform -> move the ghost to a new area -> left-click to paste -> press Esc to exit without making another paste. Ctrl+Z undoes the paste.

guides.title: 37 - Programmable custom collision zones
guides.summary: Eight named collision zones with optional solid blocking, three contact events and optional player-physics presets.
guides.notes: Tilemap Editor -> Paint collision -> choose Custom 1..8. Rename with Name Zone; friendly names are saved in the .sbgm design while generated C uses stable zone numbers 1..8. Tick Custom is solid to stop the player at the tile boundary, or untick it for walk-through zones. These tile types use collision values 9..16 (pass-through) and 17..24 (solid). They do not require extra map bytes. Paint zones directly or include these collision values in a graphical stamp. The generated maingame.c.txt contains on_custom_zone() only when a design uses custom zones AND a player sprite is named player; it registers with game_tile_set_zone_callback(). Events: GAME_ZONE_ENTERED once upon contact, GAME_ZONE_INSIDE on subsequent updates, and GAME_ZONE_EXITED upon leaving. Custom zones NEVER change physics on their own. Commented starter examples show game_tile_player_set_physics_ice/water/slow/space/floating/jetpack, game_tile_player_set_gravity and game_tile_player_set_walk_speed. Uncomment or replace only what your game needs. Physics preset normal resets to original values; overlapping zone priorities are the programmer's decision. Regenerate the game and accept the BACKUP-FIRST upgrade of the tilemap helper files. Existing main.c is never overwritten. Older SBMP v1-v4 files still load; new custom-only maps use v2 and custom+shape maps use v4, requiring the updated helper. Blocking zones can be sensed at a 1-pixel hitbox boundary; pass-through zones require overlap.
guides.example: Paint Custom 2, rename it Water, leave Custom is solid OFF. Update Game Project. In the generated on_custom_zone callback, uncomment game_tile_player_set_physics_water(p) for ENTERED and game_tile_player_set_physics_normal(p) for EXITED. A solid Custom 1 can represent a rock that reports touch while blocking movement.

guides.title: 38 - Forces, wind, explosions and zero-G thrusters
guides.summary: Impulse forces for normal movement or custom joystick-driven space motion, with full collision physics.
guides.notes: The V1 tilemap player helper exposes apply_force(&player_physics, float x, float y). X is horizontal (+right), Y vertical (+down). Units: extra PIXELS PER PHYSICS FRAME of velocity, accumulated per call and clamped for safety. Calling apply_force() does not advance the simulation; every frame call exactly ONE of game_tile_player_run(&player_physics, getjoyport(), 1) (normal joystick/jump input) or game_tile_player_step(&player_physics, 1) (no built-in joystick input). Both resolve solids, slopes, hazards, custom-zone callbacks, and external forces. One call gives an impulse, repeated calls create sustained wind or thrust. Horizontal drag is adjustable with game_tile_player_set_force_drag(&player_physics, percent): 0 means coast (ideal in zero G); normal movement defaults to 12% per frame. Vertical inertia is affected by gravity; for proper zero G set gravity to 0 when activating the space preset. The generated maingame.c.txt contains a complete OPTIONAL conditional thruster example; ordinary movement stays enabled unless you edit your main.c. Only change your existing main.c manually; Update Game Project never overwrites it. New tilemap helper files are copied by the backed-up Update Game Project process.

guides.title: 39 - Dedicated Tile Atlases in Game Resources
guides.summary: Keep PPB tile sheets under Tile Atlases instead of placing an invisible sprite on the game canvas.
guides.notes: In Game Designer, right-click the Game Resources tree and choose Add Tile Atlas... (PPB only), or drop a PPB file directly onto the Tile Atlases group. Then open Tilemap Editor and select the named PPB in the Tile Atlas dropdown. It has no canvas position, no draw call, and never creates a game sprite BOB. The .sbgm file stores the resource entry and the tilemap continues to store its PPB path; older projects and SBMP map exports remain compatible. If you have an old decorative sprite used only to hold a tilemap PPB, right-click that sprite and choose Move to Tile Atlases (stop drawing). The IDE asks before removing it from game drawing, retains the atlas path and does not touch the source PPB. Do not convert real player, object, or sprite assets: game C that refers to the old sprite variable would need updating. The tilemap dropdown continues to show the currently selected legacy sprite atlas while migrating older projects. Update Game Project regenerates gameassets to load the selected Tile Atlas PPB once from SD (or embed it, depending on generation mode). game_level1_load_atlas() borrows the matching gameassets pixels after verifying its checksum, avoiding a duplicate bitmap allocation; standalone .map/.c atlas loading still works. Only the chosen atlas is included in generated assets. The shared CLUT builder includes the chosen Tile Atlas even though it is not on the world canvas. No firmware changes, collision format changes, or tilemap helper upgrades are required. Replacing the PPB file on an active Tile Atlas resource relinks the tilemap to its new path; ensure the new artwork has compatible tile dimensions/IDs.
guides.example: Game Resources -> Add Tile Atlas... -> tiles.ppb -> Tilemap Editor -> Tile Atlas: tiles. Save the .sbgm; Update Game Project to regenerate gameassets/ and gamelevels/. For an existing project, right-click the old decorative atlas-holder sprite -> Move to Tile Atlases.

guides.title: 40 - Palette-aware PNG Import: Ranges, Dithering and Shared CLUTs
guides.summary: Convert PNG to indexed PPB using an explicit palette-index range; build or reuse a project CLUT with a live preview.
guides.notes: Right-click Game Resources > Convert PNG -> PPB. Choose Sprites, Tile Atlases or Backgrounds; choose the foreground/background CLUT where applicable (Tile Atlases use foreground; Backgrounds use background in two-plane mode and foreground in single-plane mode). The converter reserves index 0 for transparency (alpha below 50%). Specify a 1..255 range, such as 1..15 for the player, then 16..23 for scenery. Generate colours in that range, keeping the selected project CLUT entries outside the range unchanged; or match against existing colours without changing the CLUT. If starting a brand-new palette, choose Start with a blank palette. The modes are None (exact for small palettes), Floyd-Steinberg, Ordered 4x4 and Noise dither. Before/after previews use full-resolution pixels for accurate inspection: Fit to Window, 1:1 (100%), +/- buttons and mouse wheel adjust zoom without smoothing; drag either picture to pan both together. Maximizing the dialog gives both views more room. Large PNGs can take longer to update when palette settings change; saving still performs the full-resolution conversion on a background worker. Build mode writes a .pal palette file separately with an explicit filename/overwrite prompt, adds or reselects it under Palettes, and activates it for that bank. Subsequent imports can use the active .pal and a new non-overlapping index range to incrementally add artwork. The original PNG is never modified. An existing 2048-byte dual-bank .pal keeps the other bank unchanged. CAUTION: reusing/overwriting previously allocated palette indices can change colours in other existing PPBs. IDE Undo only rolls back resource-tree entries, NOT overwritten .pal/.ppb disk contents; make a backup when modifying an existing palette. PNG only (no GIF/BMP importer). No firmware changes, new map format or runtime helper changes.
guides.example: Import sprite.png: Sprites, Foreground, Generate, indices 1..15, Dither None, save sprite.ppb and gamepalettes/png_import_foreground.pal. Next import scenery.png: Tile Atlases, Generate, indices 16..23, keep existing CLUT, save scenery.ppb and update the SAME .pal. Select the generated foreground CLUT for the game and pick scenery.ppb in Tilemap Editor.
